name: Jade Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Pieter and I own Brook End, ninety hectares of sheep and vegetables, with a little farm shop by the lane. We've three hundred ewes, two polytunnels of salad and a field of leeks and squash. I'm out checking ewes by seven, then picking for the shop, then the tractor or the till. Every evening I sit with the AI planner on my laptop and sort out the grazing rotation and what the shop needs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You use AI every day? What for?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Grazing plans, shop stock, the newsletter, even working out the lambing dates from the scan results. It saves me an hour a night, easily. The thing that wears me out is the bank loan on the polytunnels, which we took two years ago and still owe most of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that the useful bits are still useful. I'll keep posting on the shop page about how the planner helps with grazing. I'd also say small farms need public support whatever the tech does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means we're back to the old squeeze. The loan on the polytunnels runs another six years, energy for the shop fridges keeps rising, and we've maybe two months of costs saved. AI saves me time, not money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the planner every night and keep the shop going. I'd try to sell more veg boxes through the shop page, aiming for forty a week instead of twenty-five, to pay the loan down faster. And I'd check if the regional farm grant covers solar panels for the shop fridges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, really. I was hoping for something that would actually change the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI saves you time, not money. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planner tells me to move the ewes to the east field on Tuesday, and it's right. But the ewes still eat the same grass and fetch the same price. A smarter grazing plan doesn't pay the polytunnel loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second-hand quad bike we were going to buy. Then our week away in June, which we've already skipped twice.

say: The useful bits of AI are **still useful**, and she'll keep saying so.
Small farms need **public support** whatever the tech does.
think: It's the old squeeze: the **polytunnel loan**, rising energy, and about **two months** saved.
do: Grow **veg box** sales from twenty-five to **forty** a week.
Apply for a **farm grant** for solar panels on the shop.
Keep using the **AI planner** every night.
feel: **Flat** and a little **disappointed** that nothing changes the numbers.
S0.quote: A smarter grazing plan doesn't pay the polytunnel loan.
fieldNote: An early adopter who already gets **time savings** but sees the **money** problem clearly.
Her existing pressure is a **six-year loan** and a thin-ish cushion.
Mixes tech enthusiasm with a firm belief in **public support** for small farms.

steps.text: Grow the farm shop veg boxes from 25 to 40 a week
Apply for the regional grant for solar panels on the shop
Keep planning grazing with the AI planner every evening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be one of the people saying this is good for small farms, if we share the tools fairly. I'd post about it on the shop page and push the local farmers' group to set up a shared account for the better software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a gift. The thinking parts of my work, the planning, the ordering, the accounts, the shop emails, are exactly what gets easier. The hands-on work stays mine for years, and robots on a hill farm come slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the bookkeeping fully onto an AI tool this year and drop our accountant's yearly fee, about nine hundred. I'd try a small weeding robot for the leeks, hired through the machinery ring, not bought. And I'd put the time I save into the shop, maybe opening a Saturday market stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Excited, with a small worry about my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worry about your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Luka tests software in the city, and that's the kind of job this eats first. I'd love him to come home and help with the shop, but I know he wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about the accountant you drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. Margaret's done our books for fifteen years. I'd tell her face to face, and I'd still want her for the tax year end, because I'm not a fool.

say: This is good for **small farms**, if the tools are **shared fairly**.
She'd push the farmers' group for a **shared software** account.
think: Planning, ordering and accounts get easier: it's **a gift** to her.
Hands-on work stays hers, as robots come **slowly** to hill farms.
do: Move the bookkeeping onto AI and save the **£900** accountant fee.
Hire a **weeding robot** for the leeks through the machinery ring.
Open a **Saturday market stall** with the time saved.
feel: **Excited**, with a small **worry** about her son's desk job.
S1.quote: My son Luka tests software in the city, and that's the kind of job this eats first.
fieldNote: Steady Disruption hits the **thinking parts** of her job, which she welcomes.
Prefers **hiring and sharing** robots over buying them outright.
Feels a pang for **Margaret**, the accountant, and for her son in software.

steps.text: Move the farm books onto an AI tool and drop the yearly accountant fee
Hire a leek weeding robot through the machinery ring
Open a Saturday market stall with the time saved
Set up a shared software account with the local farmers' group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this needs public rules and public money, fast, or the big farms with deep pockets will swallow the rest of us. I'd post it, I'd say it at the farmers' group, and I'd sign whatever petition comes along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my thinking work becomes trivial in 2028, which is fine. The danger is 2031, when the big estates get robots that do lambing and picking for pennies. Their lamb and veg prices drop, and our little shop can't match them. I'd be sixty-one, with a loan still running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get our farmers' group to form a machinery co-op this year and buy robots together, so small farms aren't left out in 2031. I'd lobby the regional council to fund it. And I'd lean harder into the shop, the farm visits and the local brand, the things a big robot farm can't copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but busy. I'd rather be worried and busy than worried and sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens on the farm in the three years between 2028 and 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are the window. The AI would plan the co-op's business, find the grants, write the bids. We'd use every hour of that to get the robots bought before the big players set the prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Mira, who studied agronomy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Mira to come home now, not in ten years, because she'd be the one running the robots. She'd laugh and say she's been telling me that for ages.

say: This needs **public rules** and **public money**, fast.
Otherwise the **big farms** swallow small ones, and she'd sign every petition saying so.
think: Her desk work becoming easy in 2028 is fine; **2031 robots** are the threat.
Big farms' **cheaper lamb and veg** would undercut the shop while the loan runs.
do: Form a **machinery co-op** with the farmers' group this year.
Lobby the **regional council** to fund the shared robots.
Lean into the **shop, farm visits** and local brand.
feel: **Worried but busy**, which she prefers to sitting still.
S2.quote: I'd rather be worried and busy than worried and sitting still.
fieldNote: She treats the **three-year gap** as a window to buy robots together.
Her income is at real risk from **big farms' prices**, so anxious despite her energy.
Wants her daughter **Mira** home to run the machines.
Blames **deep pockets**, not the technology itself.

steps.text: Form a machinery co-op with the farmers' group to buy shared robots
Lobby the regional council to fund the shared robots
Add paid farm visits and a local brand to the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to do this well, if councils and farm groups get moving. I'd be saying that at every meeting, a bit less shrill than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd likely pay off a good chunk of the polytunnel loan before the robots arrive in 2034. I'd be sixty-four then. That's a much better place to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still push the machinery co-op, but with time to do it properly and test the robots first. I'd put the time AI saves into the shop and pay down the loan faster. And I'd plan with Mira for her to take over the sheep by 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a manageable way. It feels like weather I can see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy anything yourself, outside the co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small fruit-picking robot for the polytunnels, second-hand, once the co-op has tested one. Not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the farmers' group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That five years sounds like a lot, but it's two lambing seasons of talking and three of doing. Start now.

say: Five years is **enough time**, if councils and farm groups **get moving**.
She'd say it at every meeting, **less shrill** than with the fast scenario.
think: She'd pay off much of the **loan** before robots in **2034**.
At sixty-four she'd be in a **better place** to stand.
do: Build the **machinery co-op** with time to test robots first.
Plan for **Mira** to take over the sheep by 2032.
feel: **Uneasy** but manageable, like weather she can **see coming**.
S3.quote: Five years sounds like a lot, but it's two lambing seasons of talking and three of doing.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **pay down debt** before the robot price war.
Still the organiser, now with **testing** built in.
**Succession** to Mira becomes the real plan.

steps.text: Build the machinery co-op and test robots before buying
Pay extra off the polytunnel loan each month
Plan for Mira to take over the sheep by 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty, and I'd say so. This is the one where nobody has an excuse, governments included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly good. The loan's gone by 2032, I'd be sixty-eight when the robots come, and Mira would be running the place. I'd be the old woman in the shop telling people how lambing used to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand the sheep to Mira over a few years and help the co-op buy its first robots around 2037. I'd keep the shop and the market stall as my thing. And I'd push our group to train young people on the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit proud, if it goes like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, always. And Luka's job, which might not last the ten years. But that's his to plan, and he's got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the farm look like in 2040?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2040 I see my daughter Mira, two robots, and me selling squash at the gate. I'd be happy with that.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and nobody has an **excuse**.
Governments too should use the decade to **prepare** small farms.
think: The **loan** is gone by 2032, and robots arrive when she's **sixty-eight**.
Her daughter Mira would be **running the farm** by then.
do: Hand the **sheep to Mira** over a few years.
Help the co-op buy its **first robots** around 2037.
Keep the **shop and stall** as her own work.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **proud** of the handover.
S4.quote: In 2040 I see my daughter Mira, two robots, and me selling squash at the gate.
fieldNote: A decade lets her **clear debt** and hand over before robots matter.
Only worry left is **prices** and her son's job, which she keeps at arm's length.
Pictures herself happily **in the shop**, not the fields.

steps.text: Hand the 300 ewes over to Mira over a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the big farms would get the robots and set the prices before we could get together. What would help is public money for machinery co-ops, so small farms buy robots as a group. And help with farm shops and local food, which robots can't fake.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land. Whoever owns the robots will want the land next, and small farms need rules that stop that. Small farms will survive the robots if we buy them together, and die if we buy them alone.

headlineQuote: Small farms will survive the robots if we buy them together, and die if we buy them alone.
portrait: Jade, **58**, owns a sheep and vegetable farm with a **farm shop** alongside her partner Pieter.
She uses an **AI planner** every night and welcomes help with thinking work.
A **polytunnel loan** and rising costs make her uneasy even when AI changes little.
In fast AGI she fears **big farms' prices** and answers with a machinery co-op.
With more time she plans to **hand over** to her daughter Mira and keep the shop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because big farms would get robots and set **prices** first.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for machinery co-ops so small farms buy robots together.
Support for **farm shops** and local food.
